extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers and interdisciplinary scholars working on narrative understanding and generation with LLMs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing, labeling, modeling, and evaluating narrative datasets and generation/understanding tasks using large language models. Covers dataset selection, annotation schemes, modeling choices (prompting/fine-tuning/pretraining), and evaluation metrics and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrativity as a scalar
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrativity denotes the extent to which a text exhibits qualities of narrative (temporal progression, causal linkage, presence of agents and events) and is conceptualised as a scalar property rather than a binary one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate passages with narrativity scores (degree to which text engages in narration) and aggregate to produce scalar values; examples: news report may have lower narrativity than a novel. Use these scores to test LLM detection of narrative features and to examine relationships (e.g., between narrativity and confabulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual features contributing to narrativity
rubrics_metrics.description: A taxonomy of textual features used to define narrativity, including agency, event sequencing, world building, causal relations, and rhetorical purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these features to define annotation schemes and to classify scalar narrativity or binary narrative/non-narrative; draw on literary theory (Bal, Prince, Herman). Useful when datasets contain both narratives and non-narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clause-level labeling (Labov/Berman style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotate clauses into labels such as event, subjective experience, or contextual information and identify experiencers for subjective clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to capture structural patterns within novels; inspired by socio-linguistic narrative theory. Example application: Troiano and Vossen label each clause in 19th/20th-century novels to these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporality, eventfulness, and agent-hood as labeling criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence/degree of temporality, eventfulness, and agent-hood used to measure how much a passage engages in narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these features across diverse genres (short stories, novels, Reddit posts, scientific abstracts, legal contracts) to compute narrativity scores (Piper and Bagga).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise-related evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Rate story endings on multiple surprise-related criteria (six criteria) using a 5-point Likert scale, informed by cognitive surprise, coherence, and expectation violation theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators select most and least surprising endings; criteria derive from cognitive theory (Ortony & Partridge; Brewer & Lichtenstein). Use for evaluating narrative surprise in generation/selection tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative empathy taxonomy for expert annotation
rubrics_metrics.description: A taxonomy derived from narrative empathy theory to guide expert annotations of stories (e.g., emotional/cognitive subjects, character development, perception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to structure expert labels and to evaluate dimensions like empathic engagement; applied in expert annotation work such as Shen et al. (2024b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative-writing / story-quality Likert criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Human annotation criteria for short stories using Likert scales on dimensions: relevance, coherence, empathy, surprise, engagement, and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted from interdisciplinary sources (psycholinguistics, business management, interactive storytelling). Use a 5-point Likert scale to rate each dimension when comparing human and AI-generated stories (Chhun et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation validity and inter-annotator agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess annotation validity using agreement scores and by evaluating model performance on labeled data (e.g., accuracy, precision, recall, F1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure inter-annotator agreement with Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, percent pairwise agreement, Spearman correlation. Use agreement + model metrics to validate labels and datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset construction workflow (expert-ground-truth then scale-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct datasets by having expert annotators label a subset as ground truth, then expand labels via less-experienced annotators and/or LLMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess validity via agreement and model performance. Many datasets begin expert-annotated and are extended using LLMs to increase coverage (Shen et al.; Piper et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprocessing standards for narrative corpora
rubrics_metrics.description: Common preprocessing steps: remove noise (editor's notes, image placeholders), segment into paragraphs/sentences, trim or standardize lengths, anonymise or merge character aliases, exclude minor characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprocessing choices depend on downstream tasks (e.g., merge aliases and anonymise with placeholders like [MALE]/[FEMALE]/[NEUTRAL] for character analyses). For economic reasons, use summaries (e.g., Wikipedia plot synopses) but be mindful of trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitive/harmful content filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove or reject texts containing harmful or sensitive content (sexual assault, extreme profanity) before annotation or model consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both human annotators and LLMs may reject harmful content; common in preprocessing pipelines (Shen et al. 2024b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for generation and understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated metrics commonly used: BLEU, perplexity, F1, BERTScore, BERT Similarity, inter-annotator agreement metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note limitations: BLEU has limited applicability for story generation; reference-based metrics can underestimate LLM performance and poorly align with human judgments. Complement automated metrics with human evaluations and domain-specific measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human evaluation rubric components for stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative human evaluation breaks down 'good writing' into elements such as plot, structure, character motivation, and setting; can adopt formal creative-writing assessments like the Torrance Test of Creative Writing (TTCW).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adapted grading rubrics from creative writing to evaluate GPT-generated stories against human-written baselines; combine multiple narrative elements in evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-evaluator considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs can serve as proxies for human evaluators using log-likelihood-based, prompt-based, or fine-tuned scoring methods, but they may be unreliable for evaluating individual stories while useful for comparing models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies report no significant differences among some automated LLM scoring methods in aggregate; LLM evaluators often prefer outputs from larger models and may reflect pretraining data biases. Improved scoring techniques and datasets are still needed; some work relies solely on LLM evaluation (Yu et al. 2025).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset source selection based on research aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose text sources aligned with research goals: cultural investigations (news, folktales), model-performance benchmarking (short stories), distant reading (novels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of contamination risks (models may have memorised scripts or Wikipedia summaries) and of trade-offs between original texts and summarized shorter versions for cost/length reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation and label consolidation using LLMs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use LLMs to expand annotations, consolidate multiple label outputs, and aggregate topic labels into fewer high-level labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate aggregated LLM outputs against expert annotations and treat prompt variability as comparable to human annotator variability in some contexts (Troiano & Vossen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of narratology theories in modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate classical narratology models (Propp's functions, Aristotelian three-act structure, fabula–discourse distinction) to inform narrative planning and generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these theoretical structures to guide intermediate planning steps (story functions, exposition/climax/resolution) and to computationally separate story formulation from telling (used in visual storytelling systems and prompt design).

rubrics_metrics.name: Task decomposition across narrative abstraction levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify narrative tasks by abstraction: fabula-level (event segmentation, character classification, interaction classification, event construction), discourse-level (extraction/annotation of textual features), narration-level (rhetorical intention, moral extraction, reliability classification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design datasets and models with awareness of which level a task targets; some tasks cut across levels (embedding, generation, narrativity measurement, psychological depth, cultural bias assessment, narrative reconstruction, similarity detection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection guidance: encoder vs decoder
rubrics_metrics.description: Encoder-only models (e.g., BERT) are primarily used for story-understanding tasks; decoder LLMs are used for generation, feature analysis, and classification, providing advantages in connecting low-level linguistic features to high-level theoretical constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose encoder models for classification/detection tasks and decoder models for generation and large-scale feature detection. Consider trade-offs in resources, accessibility, and task requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretraining and domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain-adaptive pretraining can be applied (continuing pretraining on folktales or target-domain corpora) but does not guarantee performance gains, especially in low-resource settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DAPT experiments may require careful tuning (epochs, batch size, learning rate) and architectural tweaks; do not assume DAPT always improves downstream narrative tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability and model openness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4) raises replicability concerns; open-weight models are valuable for reproducibility and benchmarking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers often use smaller open models (8B or lower) due to hardware constraints; quantisation and other memory-reduction techniques may be necessary for running models locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine-tuning and parameter-efficient methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine-tuning (including LoRA, distillation, instruction tuning) is effective for understanding tasks and for improving smaller models; fine-tuning for generation is less commonly reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), distillation from larger models, and masking instructions when training on completions can yield performance gains. Hardware costs motivate use of smaller models for fine-tuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt engineering best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: In-context learning (prompting) dominates narrative generation and understanding workflows; zero-shot and few-shot prompting often suffice, and simpler prompts can perform as well as complex ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zero-shot prompting is often preferred for cost and can match human annotation performance in some tasks; prompt variability can mimic human annotator variability. Preprocessing (e.g., summarisation) can sometimes harm model responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical evaluation for bias and associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use statistical analyses to detect social bias patterns (gender, race) across narratives and apply regression models to quantify associations between metrics (e.g., narrativity and hallucination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine NLP metrics and statistical tests to reveal systemic patterns; examples include logistic and beta regression linking narrativity scores with hallucination/coherence measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Output representation choices for labels and evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent annotations as scalar scores, textual labels, or vector embeddings depending on task needs (e.g., narrativity scores, textual feature labels, narrative embeddings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose representation consistent with downstream evaluation: scalar annotations facilitate quantitative analysis, textual labels support interpretability, embeddings enable similarity detection and downstream ML.
